submissions.findingTextShort: A 12-volunteer clinical PK study directly administered 12 mg asiatic acid or 24 mg asiaticoside and compared steady-state asiatic-acid exposure; this is PK, not efficacy dosing.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A clinical pharmacokinetic study in 12 healthy male and female volunteers administered approximately equimolar oral regimens of asiatic acid 12 mg or asiaticoside 24 mg and compared steady-state asiatic-acid exposure. Similar asiatic-acid AUC values were observed between the regimens because asiaticoside is converted in vivo to asiatic acid. The 12 mg and 24 mg values are study-specific PK regimens and must not be rendered as therapeutic or consumer dosing recommendations.
submissions.populationContext: Twelve healthy adult volunteers in a steady-state bioavailability study.
submissions.usageContext: Direct oral asiatic acid 12 mg versus oral asiaticoside 24 mg; pharmacokinetic comparison only.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The study establishes exposure and metabolic conversion, not wound-healing, cognitive, anti-inflammatory, or other clinical efficacy. Draft-only pending source-registry and semantic/scientific governance.

submissions.findingTextShort: Human PK shows asiaticoside is converted in vivo to asiatic acid, establishing a precursor-to-aglycone relationship rather than therapeutic interchangeability.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The human steady-state bioavailability study reports that asiaticoside undergoes hydrolytic conversion in vivo to asiatic acid. This supports a precursor/glycoside-to-aglycone relationship between asiaticoside and asiatic acid, but it does not make the two interventions therapeutically interchangeable or allow asiaticoside, Centella extract, or Madecassol outcomes to be assigned automatically to isolated asiatic acid.
submissions.mechanismContext: In-vivo hydrolytic conversion of asiaticoside to asiatic acid in humans.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Metabolic conversion is a relationship edge, not evidence inheritance across efficacy, dose, route, or safety propositions.

submissions.findingTextShort: A randomized crossover PK study measured asiatic acid after oral total triterpenic Centella fraction in healthy volunteers; the administered intervention was the extract, not isolated asiatic acid.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A randomized crossover pharmacokinetic study in 12 healthy volunteers administered the total triterpenic fraction of Centella asiatica as 30 mg or 60 mg single doses and repeated twice-daily regimens, then measured plasma asiatic acid. Repeated treatment increased asiatic-acid exposure, with the authors discussing in-vivo conversion of asiaticoside as part of the explanation. This is whole-extract exposure/metabolism evidence and cannot establish isolated-asiatic-acid efficacy or dose equivalence.
submissions.populationContext: Twelve healthy volunteers in randomized crossover single- and multiple-administration PK trials.
submissions.usageContext: Total triterpenic fraction of Centella asiatica, 30 mg or 60 mg study regimens; asiatic acid measured as analyte/metabolite.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Administered extract and measured asiatic acid are distinct evidence roles. Draft-only pending governance.

submissions.findingTextShort: A randomized phase-1 Centella product study detected asiatic acid and madecassic acid as circulating aglycones while parent glycosides were absent or minimal in plasma.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A phase-1 double-blind randomized crossover trial of a standardized Centella asiatica product in four mildly demented older adults found circulating asiatic acid and madecassic acid aglycones in plasma and urine, whereas the parent glycosides asiaticoside and madecassoside were absent from plasma or had limited renal excretion. The result supports extract-to-metabolite exposure mapping, not isolated-asiatic-acid treatment efficacy, dose equivalence, or independent acute-safety generalization.
submissions.populationContext: Four mildly demented older adults on cholinesterase-inhibitor therapy in a phase-1 standardized Centella-product PK/PD trial.
submissions.usageContext: Standardized multi-constituent Centella asiatica aqueous extract product, 2 g or 4 g single doses; asiatic acid measured as a circulating aglycone.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Product PK/PD and acute tolerability remain attached to the administered Centella formulation and tiny phase-1 sample. Draft-only pending governance.

submissions.findingTextShort: Direct human asiatic-acid evidence located here establishes pharmacokinetic exposure, not clinical benefit for wound healing, cognition, inflammation, or tissue repair.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The direct isolated-asiatic-acid human evidence located for this batch is a bioavailability/pharmacokinetic study rather than an efficacy trial. Additional human studies located here administer Centella preparations and measure asiatic acid as an aglycone or metabolite. Consequently, isolated-asiatic-acid clinical efficacy for wound healing, cognition, inflammatory conditions, tissue repair, or other therapeutic outcomes remains unestablished by these sources and should not be inferred from exposure data or parent-extract outcomes.
submissions.usageContext: Clinical-efficacy evidence gap after separating direct isolated-compound PK from parent-extract/metabolite evidence.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: This is an evidence gap, not proof of no effect. Keep NOINDEX/non-recommendation interpretation until compatible outcome evidence is separately attested.
